stories.title: Fossil fuels still absent in latest COP31 draft deal
stories.summary: A new draft agreement at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey still does not mention fossil fuels. Instead, its opening line recalls "the United Arab Emirates Consensus in its entirety" - a reference to the agreement reached in Dubai three years ago, when countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels in their energy systems. Whether those words are enough for Ireland, its EU partners and the countries that pressed for a stronger commitment is the question facing the summit this morning. The closing plenary is due to resume at 9am in Antalya (6am Irish time). The talks are now in their second day of overtime and could still end without agreement on the main text. Yesterday evening, Minister for Climate Darragh O'Brien and European Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra joined ministers and negotiators from the UK, small island states and developing countries who walked together to the COP presidency's offices.

stories.title: Triple lock Bill to include UN General Assembly clause
stories.summary: The Government intends to amend its triple lock plans to include a clause allowing the coalition to "consider" any resolution from the United Nations General Assembly relating to potential deployment, if the Bill passes the Oireachtas defence committee stage. The amendment - which has yet to receive formal Cabinet backing and will not be submitted until the triple lock plans pass through the committee and return to a final-stage vote in the Dáil and Seanad - is similar in nature to the backbench Fianna Fáil amendment submitted to the Oireachtas defence committee by former Defence Minister Willie O'Dea alongside nine other party TDs on Wednesday. However, Fine Gael sources have insisted Minister McEntee's now-confirmed amendment is not in response to the Fianna Fáil backbench pressure. "To insert a new subsection (3) to read along the following lines: "(3) Prior to any approval under paragraph (a) of subsection (2), the Government shall consider, where in existence, any resolution from the General Assembly of the United Nations or any decision of the United Nations Security Council relating to the relevant international force to which a member or contingent of the Defence Forces may, subject to this Act, be despatched for service." The key part of this newly revealed amendment is that "the Government shall consider, where in existence, any resolution from the General Assembly of the United Nations" that relates to "the relevant international force" involved in any potential future peacekeeping missions.

stories.title: Call for Govt to reverse move not to increase Carbon Tax
stories.summary: The Climate Change Advisory Council has called on the Government to reverse its decision not to increase carbon tax for the next three years. In last month's Budget, Carbon Tax on home heating oil and gas was reduced. The Government also paused a scheduled increase of Carbon Tax on petrol and diesel. At that time, Minister for Finance Simon Harris told the Dáil the rate of Carbon Tax on both kerosene and natural gas would be reduced as the recent inflated price of heating represented a heavy burden for many families who may have no easy alternatives. However, the Climate Chnage Advisory Council warned that financial pressures, limited access to alternatives and the complexity of support schemes can prevent people from taking climate action. In the final chapter of its annual review, it called on Government to "design and target climate incentives and supports around people's circumstances, making the transition to cleaner sources of energy more affordable, accessible, and straightforward".

stories.title: Bellew Group completes purchase of Solartricity
stories.summary:
Independent electrical wholesalers Bellew Group has announced it has bought solar energy business Solartricity. The Group said its part of its expansion plans in the growing renewable energy market in Ireland. Solartricity was founded in 2014 by Quentin Gargan and delivers energy solutions to customers across the UK and Ireland. The company will continue to operate under its established brand with its management team remaining in place.

The Bellew Group, which has expanded significantly in recent years through growth and acquisitions, now employs more than 300 people. The deal also follows Bellew's recent partnership with technical lighting specialist Element3. The Group described Element3's acquisition as strengthening its capabilities in lighting controls, emergency lighting and lighting distribution, particularly within the data centre market.

stories.title: Voyager 1 sends message, passes one light-day milestone
stories.summary: NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity’s first emissary to cross the monumental threshold in interstellar space. Flight controllers received the spacecraft’s call, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That is how long it took for the radio signal to traverse the more than 26 billion kilometres at the speed of light. "Travelling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveller," NASA's Heliophysics Division Director Joe Westlake said in a statement. It marked another day in the history books for Voyager 1, which launched in 1977. It also took the most distant photo of the "Pale Blue Dot" in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998, and crossed from the sun’s sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012.

stories.title: Scotstown reach Ulster final after controversial finish
stories.summary: Conor McCarthy clinched an Ulster Club SFC final spot for holders Scotstown as his clinically struck penalty secured a 4-2 shoot-out win against St Eunan's in a magnificent battle at Brewster Park. But there was huge controversy over Scotstown’s levelling point from Kieran Hughes at the end of extra-time, with replays suggesting the ball had tailed right and wide. Rory Beggan, Darren Hughes and Shane Carey were the other penalty scorers for the winners, who beat Newbridge on penalties at the same stage last year, while Niall O’Donnell and Dylan Doogan netted for Eunan’s. Kieran Donnelly and his St Eunan's players will be angered it got that far though following that Hughes free, but referee Kieran Eannetta gave the point after the umpires made no signal. The sides were level at the end of normal time after Oran Winston landed a two-pointer to tie matters on a score of Scotstown 1-18 St Eunan’s 0-21. Scotstown had the wind for the first 10 minutes in a frenetic extra-time and led by 1-21 to 0-22 at the break thanks to points from Carey, Ryan O’Toole and Nicky Sherlock with Niall O’Donnell replying with a free for Eunan’s.

stories.title: Jonathan Swift foresaw the pitfalls of AI in Gulliver's Travels
stories.summary: We think of artificial intelligence based on large language models as a discovery of our own moment, writes Daniel Carey. But Jonathan Swift – yes, the writer of Gulliver's Travels (1726) – foresaw it all in the 18th century. In our modern world we are repeatedly told by companies, governments, journalists and others that our lives can be changed through the assistance of AI. By plugging our questions into a machine and assigning it tasks of composition (from reports to books, essays, letters and even creative writing) we can sit back and let ChatGPT and its rivals do the work. Remarkable gains in knowledge and productivity are promised, based on an obscure internal architecture of algorithms that beaver away on our requests. Swift was wise to these ambitions and cast a sceptical eye on their claims. Gulliver’s Travels, his greatest satirical achievement, covers enormous ground in the objects it submits to scrutiny. The first two trips famously lead to his encounter with the petty little Lilliputians and the outsize Brobdingnagians who expose the hero to various indignities and examinations that call his assumptions into question. In his fourth and final journey, the noble Houyhnhnms – rational horses with the gift of speech – emerge as paragons for Gulliver that make him doubt the value of humanity. His third voyage, however, receives much less attention and forms no part of the popular recollection of what happens to him across his travels. Yet this sequence contains a multitude of instructive satirical occasions, one of which we could see as anticipating AI.

stories.title: A mother searches for her autistic son in Samhain
stories.summary: Line of Duty's Amy De Bhrún is the writer and star of Samhain, an acclaimed short film about a mother whose autistic son goes missing from preschool. To try to find him, she ventures into his imagination. It's a little story, beautifully told. Harry Guerin: Can you remember the moment when the idea of writing Samhain came into your head for the first time? Amy De Bhrún: Yes, I can. It was only a month or so after my son River was diagnosed with autism. I had this image of him twirling in a princess dress (something he was wearing almost every day at that point). I couldn't get that one image out of my head, and when that happens, I know I have to follow it... and so, Samhain was born! Being lost in the woods feels like a very good metaphor for how the parents of neurodivergent children might see themselves. When did that come in the writing process? Funnily enough, it wasn't straight away. It unfolded as the story did, although I felt such a strong urge to include the elements and nature in some way, so it was all connected. As you say, it's that idea of being 'lost in the woods', but yet, at the same time, if you take a deep breath, stay present, and look around you, you know exactly where you are. But you just have to trust. It's like the idea that a tree doesn't worry about its leaves shedding; it trusts that this is its process in this season of its life. How important was it for you to show people that they can romanticise the patience and resilience of the parents of neurodivergent children?

stories.title: Guterres' successor to inherit hotter world, harder task
stories.summary: After 10 years as Secretary General of the United Nations António Guterres is preparing to leave office. During his times as the helm he has addressed leaders at the opening of nine global climate summits. COP31 in Antalya is his last. Looking back at his increasingly forceful speeches reveals both anger and the limits of his office. His successor as Secretary General inherits a hotter world and a harder task. They will have better tools to tackle climate change, but less time, greater damage and the daunting challenge of bringing temperatures back down. At COP31 in Antalya this week, António Guterres confronted world leaders with the contradiction that has defined his decade at the United Nations: humanity has become much better equipped to tackle climate change, yet its response remains dangerously inadequate.

stories.title: SIPTU recommends members accept new public pay deal
stories.summary: SIPTU has recommended that its members accept the new public sector pay deal agreed with the Government. The proposals will deliver pay increases of 10.75% over two years and nine months in a deal that will run to March 2029. As part of the agreement, the threshold at which the lower-pay provisions apply will increase from €50,000 to €60,000. The cost of the draft agreement amounts to €5.2 billion and the costs will be spread over five budgets. It is composed of general round increases of 9.75% and a 1% payment for local bargaining. Local bargaining allows for pay issues to be addressed involving specific roles and grades.

stories.title: Value for many: how can architecture make everyday life better?
stories.summary: Busáras is not the obvious place to put Ireland’s architectural ambitions on the European stage. But that is precisely the point. As Ireland hosts the EU Presidency, State Architect Conor Sreenan has chosen Dublin’s landmark modernist bus station, Áras Mhic Dhiarmada, as the setting for a European Conference on Architectural Policies, turning the spotlight on the capital’s neglected north-east inner city. Meet Sreenan, and another surprise quickly emerges he is not quite what you expect a State Architect to be. Before Conor Sreenan took the helm as State Architect and Principal Architect in March 2025, his career had already spanned ambitious private practice and the thornier realities of delivering architecture in the public realm. A UCD graduate, he honed his craft at O’Donnell + Tuomey and heneghan peng before moving to the Grangegorman Development Agency as Director of Strategy & Design in 2017. Grangegorman proved formative. It was there, he says, that his instincts as a public servant took shape, and where he became convinced that the way the State commissions, procures and delivers architecture needed to change. ‘To be honest, I had very little understanding of the role of Principal Architect,’ Sreenan says, disarmingly. Perhaps understandably. The Irish State Architect is a rare creature. ‘My job has two parts to it,’ he explains. He is both an architect within government and an architectural voice for government while representing Ireland at the EU27 policy table. Curious about who else in Europe occupied comparable territory, Sreenan did some homework between accepting the job and taking it up. The answer was revealing. Just four other countries have State Architects, the Netherlands, Belgium, Estonia and Sweden. But none practises directly for the State in the Irish manner. In European terms, Ireland is an outlier. ‘I am such a proud civil servant,’ Sreenan declares, and there is no hint of irony. He regards his Assistant Secretary General grade as every bit as important as his title of State Architect. With his experience in both O’Donnell + Tuomey and heneghan peng, he is confident in his architectural judgement. ‘I’m a competent architect. I know what good looks like.’ But he now sees himself as something else too: a specialist operating within a civil service of generalists, making the case for architecture from inside the machinery of government. And he relishes it. ‘I absolutely love that stuff around accountability and democracy.’ It is also a philosophy that pushes against architecture’s stubborn cult of personality. Sreenan wants to move away from the unhealthy association of major public buildings with individual architects, historically, more often than not, men. The ambition is not to leave behind a collection of "Sreenan buildings", but a culture capable of producing good architecture long after Sreenan has left the room. ‘I want to be able to tiptoe out of here,’ he says, ‘and allow the team to continue to develop their projects.’ That meeting of architectural culture and public service was soon to be tested on a much larger stage: Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the EU, when the country would have six months to help shape priorities and steer the European policy agenda. Ireland last held this role in 2013 and will not do so again until 2040.

stories.title: Tanker struck in strait as Bahrain says Iran hit facility
stories.summary: Bahrain has accused Iran of striking a civilian industrial facility, causing a fire and damage but no casualties, while two tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz. The Gulf nation has suffered several attacks this week, ending a weeks long lull in the conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. "As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site," the interior ministry said on X, without specifying the location. "Civil Defence is working to bring the fire under control," it added. Residents told AFP they saw smoke rising over Sitra Island, on Bahrain's east coast, home to several industrial sites including a refinery run by state oil company Bapco. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said "during the operation, US military positions at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain were targeted with missile and drone strikes".

stories.title: Ireland dig deep to see off Springboks in Aviva epic
stories.summary: As they often tend to, Ireland and South Africa produced another sensational arm-wrestle, and this time it was Ireland who held out to win a gripping Nations Championship clash at Aviva Stadium. A week ago, Andy Farrell declared that his team always "stand up" when it matters, and they did that in spades as they banished the demons of last year's humiliating defeat to the Springboks, producing their best performance of the year to win a 20-17 thriller. The build-up to this game turned sour at times, but both teams allowed their rugby do the talking this evening, in the latest instalment of their recent rivalry. stories.title: Spy and sell: The murky history of economic espionage
stories.summary: The allegation that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was in a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy is undoubtedly sensational. And potentially industry-shifting. But as incredible as the story of Alice Huang may be, it's just the latest in a long line of cases, claims and accusations around China’s economic spying programme. Central to this is a belief that China has been systematically gathering information on companies, technologies and entire industries as part of the country’s broader attempt to become the world’s economic powerhouse. Because, while we tend to think of espionage as being about state secrets, political influence and military intelligence, it can also be about finding ways to gain an economic advantage on other countries. That often takes the form of trying to access research or proprietary technologies - something that’s seen as particularly attractive to China as it tries to leapfrog the likes of the US in cutting-edge areas like technology and pharmaceuticals. Though it should be said that European companies have also claimed to be the subject of Chinese spies - Germany has previously claimed to be losing tens of billions of euro and tens of thousands of jobs a year to economic espionage, with China the main culprit.

stories.title: Ireland and Australia to battle for fifth next Friday
stories.summary: Ireland will battle it out with Australia for fifth place in the inaugural Nations Championship next Friday night at Twickenham. The thrilling 20-17 victory over reigning world champions South Africa at Aviva Stadium on Saturday ensured that Andy Farrell's side finished third in the Northern Hemisphere Series behind table-toppers France and second-placed England. That means they will face Australia, the third-place finishers from the Southern Hemisphere section, in a 8.10pm kick-off in London next week. The Wallabies also won on Saturday night, beating Wales 29-26 in Cardiff. Ireland and Australia met in the opening week of the tournament in July, with the Irish side narrowly prevailing 33-31 in Sydney thanks to Thomas Clarkson's late try, converted by Sam Prendergast. Meanwhile, reigning Six Nations champions France and World Cup holders South Africa will contest the overall final on Sunday week in a repeat of their classic two rounds earlier. England face an immediate rematch against New Zealand at Twickenham on Saturday in the battle to decide third place.

stories.title: Two summits with different implications for Ukraine war
stories.summary: Two summits last Thursday - one in China, the other in Germany - had very different implications for the war in Ukraine. In Shenzhen, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States were meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit, an annual economic gathering of Asia-Pacific countries. Some in Europe were concerned that the meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin could form the basis of a Yalta-style agreement to end the war in Ukraine without either Ukrainian or European involvement. In February 1945, then US president Franklin D Roosevelt, USSR leader Joseph Stalin and UK prime minister Winston Churchill Churchill met for a summit in Yalta in Crimea and agreed upon Western and Soviet spheres of influence in Europe. For many in Poland and elsewhere in Central and Eastern Europe, the very mention of "Yalta" carries feelings of betrayal as a result. For starters, the meeting was over after 90 minutes, while the 1945 conference lasted eight days.

stories.title: Smyth signs two-year deal with New Orleans Saints
stories.summary: New Orleans Saints have signed County Down's Charlie Smyth to their main roster, the NFL club have announced, with reports suggesting it's on a two-year deal. It marks a brilliant recovery for the Mayobridge man who was released by the Saints back in August before being retained on their practice squad with New Orleans entitled to an exemption due to the international player pathway. Smyth, who had signed a three-year deal as kicker with the Saints in late 2025, was elevated back to the main roster for the NFL game against Cleveland Browns after Daniel Carlson was released. On his return, Smyth kicked three field goals, including one effort from 48 yards, as the Saints secured a 23-22 overtime victory over the Browns at the Caesars Superdome. He followed that up with an impressive 55-yard field goal against the Carolina Panthers, but they lost 20-17 on the final play. Under current NFL rules, a practice squad player can be elevated a maximum of three times per season before he has to sign a contract if he is to be used again.

stories.title: CUH row continues with substantial daylight between sides
stories.summary: On Wednesday, a row between, on the one hand, management and senior medical staff at Cork University Hospital and, on the other, senior HSE management and the Government, dominated exchanges at both the Oireachtas Health Committee and on the floor of the Dáil. What is the row about and, as winter and peak flu season approach, what is happening to resolve it? Southern Editor Paschal Sheehy traces the roots of the dispute and monitors the exchanges between both sides ... Well, it actually started many years before that, but August is as good a place to start as any. On 17 August, Cork University Hospital Chief Executive Jennifer Kearney - appointed just over a year previously - wrote to the HSE's Integrated Healthcare Area Manager for the South and West, Priscilla Lynch, to make her aware of her "increasing concern" about patient safety risks at the hospital as winter approached. The subject line was marked URGENT, and referenced "patient safety risk arising from employment approval processes".

stories.title: Cork dominate Camogie All-Stars selection
stories.summary: All-Ireland champions Cork have nine players included in the PwC Camogie All-Stars selection for 2026, with Sorcha McCartan winning the Senior Player of the Year gong. Along with McCartan, goalkeeper Amy Lee, Libby Coppinger, Méabh Cahalane, Méabh Murphy, Laura Hayes, Emma Murphy, Orlaith Cahalane and Saoirse McCarthy earned All-Stars recognition. Fellow All-Ireland finalists Galway have five players in the team: Dervla Higgins, Ciara Hickey, Carrie Dolan, Niamh McPeake and Caoimhe Kelly. Kilkenny's Niamh Deely is the only player not from Cork or Galway to make the selection. Meanwhile, Antrim's Róisín McCormick was named Intermediate Player of the Year, with Róisín O'Keeffe of Cavan winning the Premier Junior Player of the Year category. Antrim manager Elaine Dowds was awarded Camogie Manager of the Year.

stories.title: 11 killed in Mexico violence after cartel leader arrest
stories.summary: At least 11 have died after violence flared in Mexico's Sinaloa state after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, authorities have said. Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City yesterday after an intense firefight between Mexican forces and cartel members overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorised and trucks and businesses burning. Mexico's Defence Ministry said seven alleged cartel members and four Mexican soldiers were killed. Meza Flores climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltran Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organisation. The United States had a $5 million (€4.5 million) reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the US and illegally carrying firearms. Mexico's government said in a report that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.

stories.title: No gains for Maguire on day three in Florida
stories.summary: Leona Maguire was unable to make progress on Saturday after a one-over 73 in her third round at the CME Group Tour Championship. The Cavan woman had started the day 12 shots adrift of the lead but that gap is now up to 16, with Maguire tied for 49th on two-under par going into Sunday's conclusion at the Tiburon Golf Club in Florida. Maguire bogeyed 11 and 12 to slip back to one under overall. But a birdie on the third pushed her back up to two under. South Korea's A-Lim Kim leads the way by one shot on 18 under after a 69 to maintain the inside track on the $4 million (€3.65m) first prize, with Thailand's Atthaya Thitikul (67) and Yuri Yoshida (66) tied for second. American duo Auston Kim and Nelly Korda are a further stroke back on 16 under.

stories.title: Three dead, 36 missing after Indonesia factory fire
stories.summary: A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta killed at least three people while 36 others remain missing, an Indonesian rescue official said. Four people were taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic after the blaze broke out, local search and rescue agency official Rizky Dwianto said. The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in the Serang district around 50km from the capital, caught fire yesterday afternoon, a local search and rescue agency said in a statement. TV images taken overnight showed parts of the factory on fire, as some of its roof collapsed. Fires were still burning in parts of the factory this morning, complicating the search for missing victims, Mr Rizky said. "All elements of the joint SAR team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field," he added.

stories.title: U17s captain: Ireland proved a point in defeat to Brazil
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland Under-17 captain Kian Quigley says the Boys in Green's performance against Brazil in their World Cup group opener shows they can put it up to anyone. John Cotter's side impressed for vast portions of Saturday's 2-1 defeat in Qatar. After St Patrick Athletic first-team midfielder Ryan Sheridan cancelled out Brazil's opener with a well-taken equaliser, it took a wonder goal from Eduardo Conceicao to settle the contest in the South Americans' favour. And they will go into that game with confidence according to St Pat's defender Quigley after Saturday's collective display. "Brazil are one of the powerhouses of football in the world so to put it up to them, I think we should be proud of ourselves," said the Ireland skipper. "That's a lesson in itself that we're a good team. We know we're a good team so we're able to put it up to the best.

stories.summary: A four-point goal will not feature in the 2027 Allianz Football League as a number of trial rules were adopted at a meeting of the GAA's An Coiste Bainistíochta and Ard Chomhairle on Friday and Saturday. The proposal to increase the value of a goal from three points to four had been suggested by the Gaelic football's Expert Advisory Group (EAG), led by Kevin McStay, but for now it hasn't earned a spot on the 2027 Congress clár "subject to the compilation of more data." The idea of rewarding a green flag with four points was first proposed by the Football Review Committee (FRC) in 2024 as they sought to bring widespread changes to football ahead of the 2025 season. However, just prior to making their final proposals to Central Council, the enhancement was dropped and it seems now that it faces a challenge to be passed under the EAG's watch too. Goalscoring actually jumped in 2026 from the matches analysed by the GAA's games intelligence unit - from 2.1 per game in 2025 to 2.38 per game last season. stories.title: Pedestrian, 60s, dies after hit-and-run in Co Mayo
stories.summary: A pedestrian in his 60s has died after being struck by what gardaí believe was a scrambler bike in a hit-and-run in Co Mayo. The incident happened on McDermott Street in Ballina at around 9:25pm last night. Emergency services responded to the incident and the man was brought to Mayo University Hospital for treatment of serious injuries. A post-mortem examination will take place in due course, gardaí said. Garda Forensic Collision Investigators will examine the scene of the incident at Mercy Park, which is know locally as Parkside. Gardaí have appealed to any road users or local residents who may have camera footage, including dash-cam and doorbell cameras, of a scrambler bike in the area last night to make this footage available to investigating officers.

stories.title: Thousands attend protest in defence of Triple Lock
stories.summary: Thousands of people have attended a protest in Dublin city centre in support of calls to protect the Triple Lock and Irish neutrality. The protest, which began at 2pm at the Garden of Remembrance on Parnell Street before marching outside Leinster House, was organised by the Irish Neutrality League. Among the parties that attended the protest are Sinn Féin, Labour, the Social Democrats, People Before Profit-Solidarity, the Green Party and Aontú. All have called for the Government to back down on its plans to change to the Triple Lock, which they argue would risk Irish neutrality - a claim Government rejects. The Triple Lock is the system in Ireland where any deployment of 12 or more Irish Defence Forces personnel to a peacekeeping mission abroad can only take place with the permission of the Government and Dáil and with a United Nations Security Council mandate. However, due to the changing geopolitical times, Government has argued the security council has become "dysfunctional" as any one of its five permanent members - the US, China, UK, France and Russia - could potentially block Irish deployment.

stories.title: Trump proposes Miller as a presidential candidate in 2028
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump floated the idea of his new chief of staff Stephen Miller running as a candidate in the 2028 presidential election during a White House briefing. Mr Trump compared Mr Miller, an immigration hardliner, favourably to Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who stood behind them on the podium. "We have breaking news - he was better than these two guys," Mr Trump said, gesturing to Mr Vance and Mr Rubio after giving Mr Miller a turn to speak at the podium during a press conference. Mr Vance and Mr Rubio are both thought to harbour presidential ambitions, but neither individual has confirmed whether or not he will run in two years' time. Mr Trump also hailed Mr Miller - a long-time loyalist and architect of the administration's harsh deportation crackdown - as "the most powerful man in the world". The president named Mr Miller to replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff on 6 November, in the first major reshuffle following the Republican Party's hammering in the US midterm elections.

stories.title: Investigation after light aircraft lands on Sligo beach
stories.summary: Air accident investigators have launched an investigation after a light aircraft made an emergency landing on Mullaghmore Beach in Co Sligo this afternoon. The RNLI said it received what it called "reports of a light aircraft crash" on the beach with two people understood to be on board. A lifeboat was launched at 2.21pm following a request from the Irish Coast Guard at Malin and arrived on the scene shortly after. The RNLI crew assessed the situation alongside An Garda Síochána, the National Ambulance Service and other emergency services attending the incident. The lifeboat was stood down at 2.45pm, with nobody requiring assistance. Gardaí said that the pilot and passenger - men aged in their 30s and 20s - were uninjured.
